title: Leonidas at Thermopylae
text:
In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with an enormous army. A small Greek force of a few thousand men, led by the Spartan king Leonidas with his bodyguard of three hundred Spartans, took position at Thermopylae, a narrow pass between the mountains and the sea.

Herodotus tells how for two days the Greeks held the pass against wave after wave of attacks, including the king's elite troops. Then a local man, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path that led around behind the Greek position.

When Leonidas learned he was about to be surrounded, he sent most of the allied contingents away. Herodotus says Leonidas stayed with his three hundred Spartans, the seven hundred Thespians who refused to leave, and a contingent of Thebans. Herodotus adds that an oracle had told the Spartans that either Sparta would be destroyed or a Spartan king would die.

On the third day the remaining Greeks fought in the open until they were overwhelmed. Leonidas was killed, and they fought over his body. The Spartans and Thespians died almost to a man; the Thebans, Herodotus says, surrendered. An epitaph later set up there asked the passerby to tell the Spartans that their men lay there, obedient to their orders.
lesson: Standing by a hard commitment, and releasing others who need not share it, can give your example a meaning that lasts for generations.
people: Leonidas I of Sparta, Xerxes, Ephialtes
caveat: Herodotus's figures for the Persian army are impossibly large, and his account of the Thebans' role is disputed.
